analysis.one_liner: Makes public college tuition-free for working- and middle-class students and roughly doubles Pell Grants.
analysis.headline: The College for All Act drew 67 Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote in any of its three committees, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would send federal money to states, tribal colleges, and historically Black and minority-serving institutions to wipe out tuition and fees — for everyone at community colleges, and for students from families making up to $125,000 (single) or $250,000 (married) at public four-year schools. It would also roughly double the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790, let students use it for living expenses, and make undocumented 'Dreamer' students eligible. The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at community colleges — tuition-free regardless of income — and working- and middle-class students at public four-year universities (family incomes up to $125,000 single or $250,000 married). Low-income students gain from a doubled Pell Grant ($14,790 max) usable for living expenses and a longer eligibility window. Dreamer students gain Pell eligibility. Students at private HBCUs and minority-serving institutions gain tuition elimination, and tuition is waived for students from outlying territories like Guam and American Samoa.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, and for students from families earning up to $125,000 (single) or $250,000 (married) at public four-year institutions, through a federal-state partnership.

Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790 for 2024-25 (about double the prior level), extends eligibility to 7.5 years instead of 12 semesters, allows the grant to cover living and non-tuition expenses, and expands eligibility to Dreamer students.
Funds tuition elimination at private nonprofit historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions for income-eligible students.

Requires participating states to maintain their own higher-education funding, keep instruction spending from falling, and move toward 75% tenure-track faculty — attaching quality protections to the money.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations ('such sums as may be necessary') with no funding source specified in the bill — the tuition-free program alone is estimated to cost tens of billions per year. States must contribute a growing state share (rising to 20% by 2028-29) and are barred from cutting their own higher-education spending below a three-year average. Colleges charging above-average tuition in high-cost states get supplemental federal aid.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes and appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' each year through 2033 with no revenue source, so the full cost would fall on federal borrowing or future tax choices left unspecified in the bill.

The four-year tuition waiver reaches families earning up to $250,000 (married couples), a threshold well above the median household income, which critics would call far broader than 'working- and middle-class.'

States must permanently commit their own money — up to 20% of the cost plus a maintenance-of-effort floor — which some states could not or would not accept, raising the risk of uneven adoption across the country.

Requiring other student aid to be applied only to living costs, and capping out-of-state charges at marginal cost, would force colleges to rework their budgets and could squeeze institutions in high-cost states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: tuition-free community college for everyone and debt-free or tuition-free four-year public college for most families, plus a doubled Pell Grant. The cost is genuinely open-ended — the bill names no funding source and commits the federal government to a permanent entitlement, with states locked into their own spending floors. An honest supporter would acknowledge the price tag is a major fiscal commitment left to future Congresses, and that the $250,000 income cap is generous. The design does include real safeguards (maintenance of effort, tenure-track targets, bans on using funds for stadiums or administrator salaries), which is more discipline than many spending bills contain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the College for All Act of 2023 in the House on June 14, 2023.
The same day, it was referred to the Committees on Education and the Workforce, Budget, and Ways and Means.
Sixty-seven House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republicans signed on.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral — the bill never advanced at all.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges that charge tuition — including for-profit colleges excluded from the bill and private institutions that would have lost enrollment to free public options — are better off, as are student loan lenders whose business depends on tuition debt. Fiscally conservative members who preferred not to take a vote on a large new entitlement also got the outcome they wanted without having to vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tuition-charging colleges and student loan lenders

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the College for All Act on June 14, 2023 and recruited 67 cosponsors.

for.name: 67 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Pressley, Tlaib, and Nadler
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican joined, and no committee action followed.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.role: First-referral committee; chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup was held after the June 2023 referral.

against.name: House Budget and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Also took no action on the bill after referral.

against.name: House Republican majority leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor schedule in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote, consistent with the majority party's opposition to large new federal spending programs; the bill had zero Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 68 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican majority that controlled the House committees and floor never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would make public two- and four-year institutions the permanent, federally funded channel for tuition-free college, locking in a federal-state funding stream through them while also imposing quality rules (tenure-track floors, instruction-spending floors). Students and the institutions win together.
Tuition-free public college and a doubled Pell Grant would sharply reduce how much students need to borrow, cutting demand for private student loans and shrinking federal loan volume.

The bill excludes for-profit institutions from its tuition grants entirely and bars institutions that converted from for-profit to nonprofit status from eligibility for at least 25 years, while free public options would pull away their prospective students.

Private HBCUs and minority-serving institutions would receive tuition-elimination grants, but other private nonprofit colleges would compete against a free public alternative and lose enrollment — though some also enroll students who benefit from the Pell expansion.
